sections.heading: SOUL DUST TO REVIVAL
pulls: You will never love a force. You can only love a Person. The Spirit is a He, and until a man knows that, he will keep trying to use what he was meant to know.
paras: Before you walk with the Holy Spirit for twelve weeks, one thing has to be settled that most men have never settled: who the Spirit is. Not what. Who. Because a man will relate to a force very differently than he relates to a Person, and most men, if they are honest, have quietly thought of the Spirit as an it — an energy, an influence, a power to be tapped when needed and forgotten the rest of the time.

But Jesus never speaks of the Spirit that way. Listen to how He talks in the upper room: He will teach you. He will guide you. He will remind you. He will glorify Me. Over and over, when the grammar could have gone either way, Jesus reaches for He. The Spirit is not a divine battery. He is a Person — the third Person of the Trinity — with a mind that knows, a will that chooses, and a heart that can be grieved. You do not tap a Person. You know Him.

This is where the dust starts to lift. A man clinging to the dirt does not most deeply need more power; he needs a Person who is already with him, already in him, already at work. Revive me according to Your word is not a request for a jolt of energy. It is a cry that God answers by His own indwelling Spirit — a Someone, not a something, who moves into a man to make him alive. The whole study depends on getting this right. He is not an it.

sections.heading: WHAT THIS WEEK IS AFTER
paras: This week goes after a relationship with the Spirit, not a technique for using Him. A great deal of confusion in a man’s life with God comes from treating the Spirit like electricity — something to plug into for a result. Scripture will not allow it. The Spirit speaks, leads, teaches, forbids, appoints, grieves, and intercedes. Those are the actions of a Person, and a man is meant to walk with Him as one.

The goal this week is simply to meet the Spirit as He — to stop saying “it” in your heart and start relating to the Someone God has put within you. One fact will steer this entire study: the Spirit, this Person, has a defining passion, and it is not Himself. It is Christ. “He will glorify me,” Jesus says. The Spirit is the most self-effacing Person in the universe. He came not to draw attention to Himself but to make much of Jesus — and that single fact will keep you out of every ditch a study of the Spirit can fall into.

sections.heading: WHY THESE PASSAGES
paras: Because in John 14 and 16, Jesus does the very thing many teachers avoid: He assigns the Spirit personal pronouns and personal actions, on purpose. He calls Him the Counselor — a title for a person, not a power. And in Romans 8, Paul shows the Spirit doing the most personal thing imaginable: praying, interceding, searching hearts, carrying a man’s wordless groans to the Father. A force does not intercede. A Person does. Put these together and the conclusion is unavoidable: the Holy Spirit is God Himself, personally present, personally at work, personally near.

sections.heading: The Man Who Uses Instead of Knows
paras: You know the pattern, because most men have lived it. A man hits a wall — a temptation he cannot beat, a decision he cannot make, a dryness he cannot shake — and he reaches for the Spirit like a tool: give me power, give me a sign, get me through. And when the crisis passes, he sets the tool back down and goes on as before. He has treated a Person like an appliance. And he wonders why his life with God feels thin, transactional, cold. It is because you cannot have a relationship with a thing you only use. The Spirit is not waiting to be deployed. He is present to be known — and the man who learns to know Him, rather than use Him, finds the dryness starting to lift.

parts.label: PART ONE
parts.heading: The Counselor Is a Someone
paras: Start with the name Jesus chooses. He does not call the Spirit “the power” or “the influence.” He calls Him the Counselor — the one called to a man’s side. That is relational language from the first syllable. You are helped by a person, not by a current. And Jesus deepens it: this Counselor will teach, will remind, will guide into all truth, will speak what He hears, will declare what is to come. Every one of those verbs requires a mind and a will. Forces do not teach. Persons teach.

This matters more than it may first seem, because a man’s whole posture changes with it. Toward a force, a man is a user — he reaches for it to get an outcome and lets go when he is done. Toward a Person, a man is a companion — he listens, he responds, he does not want to grieve the One who is always there. Ephesians says exactly that: do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God. You cannot grieve electricity. You can only grieve Someone who loves you. The Spirit is that Someone.

And listen to how personally Jesus frames the Spirit’s coming in that same upper room. He does not say I will leave you a force to compensate for My absence. He says the opposite: “I will not leave you orphans. I will come to you.” The gift of the Spirit is Jesus’ answer to abandonment — the promise that His people will never be fatherless, never be left alone. He tells them the Spirit “lives with you, and will be in you,” and even more astonishingly, that when a man loves Him and keeps His word, “We will come to him, and make our home with him.” That is not the language of a power being dispatched. It is the language of a Person — indeed of the Father and the Son by the Spirit — moving in to stay. The Counselor does not visit the orphan. He ends the orphanhood by taking up residence.

This is why the personhood of the Spirit is not a doctrinal technicality but a lifeline for a lonely man. The deepest ache under a great deal of the dust is a felt fatherlessness — a sense of being on one’s own, unaccompanied, unseen. And Jesus aims the promise of the Spirit precisely at that ache: you are not orphans; He lives with you and will be in you; the Father and the Son will make their home with you. A force could never touch that loneliness. Only a Person can. And the Spirit is that Person, sent to make sure no child of God is ever left alone.

parts.label: PART TWO
parts.heading: A Person You Can Grieve — and a Person Who Prays
paras: Two things Scripture says about the Spirit settle His personhood beyond argument, and both are tender. The first: He can be grieved. “Don’t grieve the Holy Spirit of God, in whom you were sealed for the day of redemption.” Grief is not a mechanical reaction; it is the response of a heart to being wounded by someone it loves. That the Spirit can be grieved means the Spirit has affections — that your sin is not merely the breaking of a rule but the wounding of a Person who dwells in you and loves you. That reframes holiness entirely. It is not rule-keeping. It is not grieving Someone near.

The second: He prays. In Romans 8, when a man is so weak he does not even know what to ask, “the Spirit himself makes intercession for us with groanings which can’t be uttered.” Read that slowly. The Spirit Himself. Interceding. Praying, inside a man, on his behalf, carrying to the Father what the man cannot put into words. A force cannot intercede. Intercession is the most personal act of love there is — standing between someone you love and their need. The Spirit does this for you, right now, in the places too deep for your own words to reach.

Put it together and the picture is overwhelming: the God of the universe has not sent a power into you. He has come Himself, as a Person, to dwell in you, to be grieved by what wounds you, to pray in you when you cannot pray, and — above all — to make Jesus real to you. This is who you are walking with for twelve weeks. Not an it. A He. And this He is entirely devoted to showing you Christ.

stations.verse: I will pray to the Father, and he will give you another Counselor, that he may be with you forever: the Spirit of truth, whom the world can’t receive; for it doesn’t see him and doesn’t know him. You know him, for he lives with you, and will be in you. I will not leave you orphans. I will come to you.
note: Every phrase is personal. Another Counselor — sent by the Father at the Son’s request, taking up the place Jesus Himself had filled beside the disciples. You know Him — you do not know a force; you know a Someone. He lives with you and will be in you — residence, not a visit. And the aim of it all: “I will not leave you orphans.” The Spirit is Jesus’ answer to abandonment, His promise that His people are never left alone. A force cannot end an orphan’s loneliness. Only a Person can.
stations.question: Where in your life do you most feel like an orphan, left to carry things on your own?
stations.gloss: an orphan, fatherless; in a wider sense, bereft, friendless, desolate
stations.live: Name the place where you feel most alone this week. Say John 14:18 out loud there, and speak to the Spirit as the One who is present in it.
body: Orphanos is the word for a child with no father to stand for him. James uses it for the fatherless the church must care for (James 1:27). In John 14:18 Jesus uses it of men about to lose their Teacher: “I will not leave you orphans.” The promise does not stand alone. It stands on the verse before it, where the Father gives “another Counselor” who lives with them and will be in them. The cure for being bereft is a Person moving in. When Jesus went away, He did not leave you with a memory or a manual. He left you with Someone.

stations.verse: However when he, the Spirit of truth, has come, he will guide you into all truth, for he will not speak from himself; but whatever he hears, he will speak. He will declare to you things that are coming. He will glorify me, for he will take from what is mine, and will declare it to you.
note: The Spirit’s mind and His mission come in one breath. He guides — a personal act. And He glorifies Christ — His defining passion. Jesus says plainly what the Spirit is always doing: taking what belongs to the Son and declaring it to you. The most personal Being has the most Christ-centered agenda. He does not point to Himself. He points to the Son.
stations.question: When you ask the Spirit for help, are you asking Him to show you Christ, or to give you an experience?
stations.gloss: to lead on one’s way, to guide; figuratively, to guide, instruct, teach
stations.live: Before you open your Bible each morning this week, ask plainly: “Spirit of truth, guide me into what You want me to see of Christ here.”
body: Hodēgeō is road language — leading someone along a way. The Ethiopian in his chariot uses it: “How can I, unless someone explains it to me?” (Acts 8:31). Jesus uses it of the Spirit: “he will guide you into all truth.” A guide walks the road with you. He does not hand you a map and wish you well. The Spirit guides the way a man leads another through country he knows, and the country is the truth about Christ. A map cannot walk beside you. The Spirit does.

stations.verse: In the same way, the Spirit also helps our weaknesses, for we don’t know how to pray as we ought. But the Spirit himself makes intercession for us with groanings which can’t be uttered.
note: The Spirit prays. Not a force, not a feeling — “the Spirit himself,” making intercession. This is the most personal act there is: standing in the gap for someone in his weakness. When a man is too worn to form words, the Spirit is not idle within him. He is praying, carrying the man’s wordless ache to the Father.
stations.question: Where are you too weak right now to know what to pray?
stations.gloss: inexpressible, not to be uttered
stations.live: Set aside five quiet minutes this week with no words at all. Tell God only this: “Spirit, pray for me what I cannot say.”
body: Alalētos appears once in the New Testament, right here. It is built from lalēo, to speak, with a negative in front: what cannot be spoken. WEB renders it “groanings which can’t be uttered.” Paul does not say the Spirit’s prayer is vague. He says it goes where words cannot. When your own prayer runs out of words, the Spirit’s does not run out of love. He carries the ache you cannot name to the Father who searches hearts (8:27). Your silence in prayer is not the end of prayer. It may be where the Spirit is praying hardest.

stations.verse: Don’t grieve the Holy Spirit of God, in whom you were sealed for the day of redemption.
note: You can grieve Him. Only a person can be grieved — it is the wound of a heart that loves. Paul does not say do not short-circuit the Spirit or drain the Spirit; he says do not grieve Him. Your sin is not merely rule-breaking. It wounds a Person who lives in you, loves you, and has sealed you as His own. Holiness, seen this way, is tenderness toward Someone near.
stations.question: Which sin in your life have you treated as a broken rule rather than a grieved Person?
stations.gloss: to distress, to grieve, to cause pain or grief
stations.live: Pick the one sin you most easily excuse. Each time it pulls at you this week, say: “This would grieve the Spirit who sealed me.”
body: Lypeō is the word for real sorrow. Matthew uses it of Jesus in Gethsemane: He “began to be sorrowful and severely troubled” (Matthew 26:37). Paul uses it of the Spirit: “Don’t grieve the Holy Spirit of God.” You cannot sadden a force. You can only sadden Someone who cares. The same verse says you were sealed in Him — so the One your sin grieves is the One who has already marked you as His own and will not let you go. The Spirit can be grieved because He has a heart. Guard it, because He guards you.

stations.verse: When they had gone through the region of Phrygia and Galatia, they were forbidden by the Holy Spirit to speak the word in Asia. When they had come opposite Mysia, they tried to go into Bithynia, but the Spirit didn’t allow them.
note: The Spirit has a will. Paul and his men had a plan and a map, and the Spirit said no — twice. “Forbidden by the Holy Spirit,” then “the Spirit didn’t allow them.” A force does not forbid anything. It has no mind about where a man goes. The Spirit does. He opens and He shuts, and a closed road in Luke’s account is not bad luck. It is a Person steering His servants toward Macedonia, where the next door was already waiting.
stations.question: What closed door in your life might be the Spirit steering you rather than God abandoning you?
stations.gloss: to hinder, to restrain, to forbid, to withhold
stations.live: Look back at one door God closed in your past. Write one sentence about what He opened on the other side of it.
body: Kōlyō means to stop someone or keep him from going ahead. Jesus uses it when the disciples try to keep the children away: “Don’t forbid them” (Matthew 19:14). Luke uses it of the Spirit: Paul and his team “were forbidden by the Holy Spirit to speak the word in Asia.” Only a Person can forbid. The Spirit has a mind about where His men go, and a no from Him is guidance, not rejection. Macedonia was on the other side of that closed door. A no from the Spirit is still the Spirit leading you.

practices.title: CATCH THE “IT”
practices.body: This week, notice every time you think of the Spirit as a force, a feeling, or a power to use — and gently correct it. Say it out loud if you need to: “He. Not it. A Person.” Begin addressing Him directly in prayer, as you would the Father or the Son: “Holy Spirit, You are here. Teach me. Lead me today.” The change in language will begin to change the relationship.

practices.title: GUARD HIS HEART
practices.body: Pick the one area where you most easily justify sin, and this week reframe it entirely. Not “I am breaking a rule,” but “I am grieving the Person who lives in me and loves me.” Let that tenderness, not mere willpower, be what pulls you back. Holiness born of not wanting to grieve Someone near lasts longer than holiness born of guilt.

practices.title: ASK HIM FOR CHRIST
practices.body: Since the Spirit’s great passion is to glorify Jesus, spend this week asking Him for exactly that: “Spirit, make Christ real to me. Show me the Son.” Do not seek an experience of the Spirit apart from Jesus. Seek the Jesus the Spirit loves to reveal. Watch whether Christ becomes larger to you as the week goes on.

practices.title: LISTEN BEFORE YOU PLAN
practices.body: The Spirit forbade Paul’s plan and then led him somewhere better. This week, before one real decision — a purchase, a conversation, a schedule change — stop and pray: “Spirit, You have a will. Show me Yours before I settle mine.” Then wait a day before you act, and notice what He brings to mind from Scripture.

practices.title: SAY HIS NAME
practices.body: The Spirit is the Counselor Jesus promised, not a vague presence. Each night this week, before you sleep, thank Him by name for one specific thing He did that day — a verse that came back, a temptation you refused, a word you held back. Keep it short. The point is to know Him, not to perform for Him.

title: He, Not It
subtitle: the Spirit is a Person, not a force
keyVerse: But the Counselor, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, will teach you all things, and will remind you of all that I said to you.

passage.text: If you love me, keep my commandments.
I will pray to the Father, and he will give you another Counselor, that he may be with you forever:
the Spirit of truth, whom the world can’t receive; for it doesn’t see him and doesn’t know him. You know him, for he lives with you, and will be in you.
But the Counselor, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, will teach you all things, and will remind you of all that I said to you.

However when he, the Spirit of truth, has come, he will guide you into all truth, for he will not speak from himself; but whatever he hears, he will speak. He will declare to you things that are coming.
He will glorify me, for he will take from what is mine, and will declare it to you.
In the same way, the Spirit also helps our weaknesses, for we don’t know how to pray as we ought. But the Spirit himself makes intercession for us with groanings which can’t be uttered.
He who searches the hearts knows what is on the Spirit’s mind, because he makes intercession for the saints according to God.

stationsIntro: The verses below establish, from Jesus’ own mouth and Paul’s own pen, that the Holy Spirit is a Person — He teaches, guides, wills, can be grieved, and intercedes. Read each slowly. Let the commentary land before you answer. Then sit with the word study beneath it. The thread this week runs from an it to a He — from a force a man uses to a Person a man comes to know.
lifeIntro: This week is about a shift in posture — from using the Spirit to knowing Him, from it to He. The point of Week 1 is to begin relating to the Spirit as the Person He is. Five practices for the next seven days.
prayer: Holy Spirit, You are not a force. You are the Lord, and You are here. I have used You like a tool and set You down when I was done. Forgive me. Teach me to know You. Guide me into the truth, and let that truth be Christ. When I cannot pray, pray for me. When I am tempted to grieve You, remind me that You sealed me. Father, thank You for not leaving me an orphan. Jesus, show me Your face today by Your Spirit. Amen.
prayerLines: Holy Spirit, You are not a force. You are the Lord, and You are here.
I have used You like a tool and set You down when I was done.
Forgive me. Teach me to know You.
Guide me into the truth, and let that truth be Christ.
When I cannot pray, pray for me.
When I am tempted to grieve You, remind me that You sealed me.
Father, thank You for not leaving me an orphan.
Jesus, show me Your face today by Your Spirit. Amen.
bottomLine: The Holy Spirit is a He, not an it. He teaches, guides, forbids, can be grieved, and prays for you when you cannot. Jesus did not leave you an orphan. He sent a Person to live in you and to show you Christ.
benediction: Brother, for twelve weeks you are going to walk with the Holy Spirit — and everything depends on how you begin. Most men begin wrong. They come to the Spirit the way they come to a tool: to be used in a crisis and shelved in the calm. And they wonder why their life with God stays cold and thin. It stays cold because you cannot warm yourself on a thing you only use. The Spirit was never meant to be used. He was meant to be known.

Because the Spirit is not an it. He is a He — the third Person of the Trinity, God Himself, personally present within you. He teaches. He guides. He speaks. He appoints. He can be grieved, because He has a heart. He intercedes, because He loves. And His deepest passion, the thing that defines Him, is not to make much of Himself but to make much of Jesus. He is the most self-effacing Person in existence, and He came to live in you and turn your face, again and again, toward Christ.

So as you begin, lift up your eyes. Lift them off the force you have been trying to use and onto the Person who is already with you, already in you, already praying for you with groanings no words can carry. Lift them off your cold, transactional religion and onto the warm nearness of Someone who can be grieved and longs not to be. And lift them, as He Himself would have you do, onto Christ — because the Spirit’s whole aim is to make the Son large in your sight, and a man who meets the Spirit rightly always ends up seeing more of Jesus.

You do not have a force at your disposal. You have a Person at your side and within your chest. Learn His name. Guard His heart. Ask Him for Christ. And let the God who lives in you begin, this week, to lift you out of the dust — not as a power you wield, but as a Person you are finally coming to know.
closingVerse: The Spirit is not something God gives you to use. He is Someone God gives you to know — and knowing Him, you will not be able to stop seeing Christ.
carry: If the Spirit is a Person living in you, what would you say to Him today?

sections.heading: SOUL DUST TO REVIVAL
pulls: The Spirit is a floodlight, and Christ is the cathedral. Stop staring at the light. Let it show you the Son — that is the light doing exactly what it came to do.
paras: Week 1 met the Spirit as a He, not an it — a Person, not a force. This week asks the most important question of the entire study: what does this Person most want to do? Because a lot of men, once they realize the Spirit is real and personal, start chasing the Spirit for His own sake — hunting experiences, sensations, power, goosebumps. And they end up frustrated, because they are seeking the Spirit in a way the Spirit Himself will not cooperate with.

The reason is simple. The Spirit has a defining passion, stated by Jesus in the plainest words: “He will glorify me.” The Spirit’s central mission is not to make you feel Him. It is to make you see Christ. He is like a floodlight aimed at a cathedral — you are not supposed to stare at the light; you are supposed to see what the light reveals. A floodlight doing its job draws no attention to itself. Neither does the Spirit. His whole joy is to take what belongs to Jesus and make it real, vivid, and precious to you.

This changes how a man seeks Him. Revive me according to Your word is answered by the Spirit, but the Spirit answers it by lifting up Christ. A man who wants to be revived does not go looking for the Spirit in the abstract. He asks the Spirit to show him Jesus — and finds, in seeing Jesus, that he is being revived. The dust lifts not when a man feels a surge of spiritual electricity, but when the Spirit makes the Son so real that the dirt loses its grip.

sections.heading: WHAT THIS WEEK IS AFTER
paras: This week goes after Christ, by the Spirit — which is the only way the Spirit wants to be sought. There is a subtle error that traps sincere men: making the Spirit the destination instead of the guide. But the Spirit is not the destination. Christ is. The Spirit is the One who takes you there. When a man makes the Spirit an end in Himself, he grieves the very Spirit he is chasing, because the Spirit’s joy is to be the means by which Christ is seen, not the object of the staring.

The goal this week is to reorient every desire for the Spirit toward its true aim: seeing, knowing, loving, and becoming like Jesus. This is not a lesser use of the Spirit; it is His highest use, the one He delights in. And it is the safeguard of the whole study — because a Spirit-seeking that does not lead to Christ has gone wrong somewhere, and a Christ-seeing that grows week by week is the surest evidence the Spirit is genuinely at work.

sections.heading: WHY THESE PASSAGES
paras: Because they say the same thing from four angles. In John 15, the Spirit testifies about Christ. In John 16, He glorifies Christ and declares what is Christ’s. In 1 Corinthians 12, it is only by the Spirit that a man can even say Jesus is Lord. And in 2 Corinthians 3, the Spirit is the One who unveils a man’s face to behold the glory of the Lord, transforming him into that same image. Witness, glorify, confess, transform — every one of them is the Spirit turning a man toward the Son. There is no ambiguity in Scripture about the Spirit’s central agenda. It is Christ.

sections.heading: The Man Chasing the Wind
paras: You know the temptation, especially for an earnest man. He hears that the Spirit is strong, personal, alive — and he starts chasing the sensation of the Spirit. He goes from conference to conference, worship high to worship high, chasing the feeling, and each one fades faster than the last. He is chasing the wind, and he cannot catch it, because he is seeking the Spirit in a way the Spirit will not bless — as an end instead of a guide. The moment that same man stops chasing the feeling and starts asking the Spirit to show him Jesus, everything changes. The wind he could not catch begins, quietly, to fill his sails — because now he is going the direction the Spirit was always blowing: toward Christ.

parts.label: PART ONE
parts.heading: The Witness Who Testifies to Another
paras: In John 15, Jesus describes the Spirit’s work with a courtroom word: He will bear witness about Me. A witness does not testify about himself; by definition, a witness points away from himself to another. That is the Spirit’s posture. He takes the stand not to describe His own glory but to testify to the glory of Christ. The Spirit is the greatest witness who ever lived, and His entire testimony is: look at the Son.

This is why a genuine experience of the Spirit always enlarges Jesus in a man’s eyes. When the Spirit moves on a heart, the result is not I felt the Spirit so much as I saw Christ — His mercy became real, His cross became weighty, His nearness became undeniable. If a spiritual experience leaves a man impressed with the experience but not more in love with Jesus, something has gone sideways. The Spirit’s witness always lands on Christ. That is how you know it is Him.

Jesus presses this even further in the same discourse, and it is startling: “It is to your advantage that I go away, for if I don’t go away, the Counselor won’t come to you.” Think about that. The disciples had Jesus in the flesh, walking beside them — and He says it is better for them that He leave, because then the Spirit will come. Why better? Because the Spirit does something the physical presence of Jesus, localized in one place, could not: He makes Christ real and present to every believer everywhere, at once, forever. The Spirit is not a consolation prize for Jesus’ absence. He is the way Jesus becomes nearer than He ever was on the roads of Galilee — present now not beside you but within you, making the Son real from the inside.

And notice what Jesus says the Spirit will do when He comes: He will convict the world concerning sin and righteousness and judgment. Even the Spirit’s convicting work is aimed at Christ. He convicts the world of sin, Jesus says, because they do not believe in Me; of righteousness, because I go to the Father; of judgment, because the ruler of this world is judged. Every stroke of conviction points to Jesus — His person, His vindication, His victory. The Spirit does not convict a man merely to make him feel bad; He convicts to turn a man’s eyes to Christ, to expose the emptiness of life apart from Him and the mercy available in Him. Even the sharp work of the Spirit is Christ-ward. He wounds only to point to the One who heals.

parts.label: PART TWO
parts.heading: Beholding, and Being Changed
paras: The clearest description of how the Spirit works is in 2 Corinthians 3. Paul says that when a man turns to the Lord, the veil is removed, and then: “we all, with unveiled face seeing the glory of the Lord as in a mirror, are transformed into the same image from glory to glory.” For this comes from the Lord who is the Spirit. Read the mechanism carefully, because it is the engine of all Christian change.

The Spirit does not transform a man by making him stare at himself and try harder. He transforms a man by unveiling his face to behold the glory of the Lord — to see Christ — and in the beholding, the man is changed into what he beholds. This is how the dust lifts. Not by a man gritting his teeth at his own sin, but by the Spirit lifting his eyes to Jesus until, looking at the Son, he slowly becomes like the Son. You become what you behold. And the Spirit’s whole work is to hold Christ before your face so that beholding Him, you are remade.

This is the answer to every man exhausted by self-improvement. You were never meant to change by looking harder at yourself. You were meant to change by beholding Christ, and the Spirit is the One who unveils your face to see Him. The transformation is real — “from glory to glory” — but it comes not from staring at the mirror of your own effort. It comes from the Spirit turning your gaze to the Son. Behold Him, and be changed. That is the Spirit’s design, and it is gentle, and it works.

stations.verse: He will glorify me, for he will take from what is mine, and will declare it to you.
note: The Spirit’s mission statement, from Jesus’ own lips. His work is to glorify Christ — to take what belongs to the Son and declare it to you. The Spirit is not building His own name; He is magnifying the Son’s. This is the compass for everything: wherever the Spirit is truly at work, Christ grows larger, clearer, more precious. If Jesus is fading from view, whatever else is happening, it is not the Spirit’s doing.
stations.question: Is Jesus growing larger or smaller in your sight lately?
stations.gloss: to magnify, to extol, to praise; in the LXX and NT, to clothe with splendor, to glorify
stations.live: At the end of each day this week, write down one way Christ looked larger to you than He did that morning.
body: Doxazō comes from doxa, glory. Jesus uses it for the light a man’s good works cast back on the Father (Matthew 5:16), and in His last prayer: “Father, the time has come. Glorify your Son” (John 17:1). Of the Spirit He says, “He will glorify me.” The Spirit spends no effort on His own reputation. Every bit of His work goes to making the Son’s worth seen. That is how you can tell His voice from any other: it makes Jesus larger. A man in step with the Spirit is not preoccupied with the Spirit. He is preoccupied with Christ.

stations.verse: When the Counselor has come, whom I will send to you from the Father, the Spirit of truth, who proceeds from the Father, he will testify about me.
note: The Spirit is a witness, and a witness points away from himself. His testimony is not about His own power or presence; it is “about me” — about Christ. He comes from the Father, sent by the Son, and He speaks of the One who sent Him. When the Spirit moves on a heart, the verdict is always the same: look at the Son. Real encounters with the Spirit leave a man more in love with Jesus, not merely impressed with an experience.
stations.question: When you have sought spiritual experiences, did they leave you more in love with Jesus?
stations.gloss: to go out, to go forth, to proceed
stations.live: When you pray this week, pray to the Father, in the name of the Son, by the Spirit — and notice that the Spirit leads your praying toward Christ.
body: Ekporeuō is the plain verb for something going out from a source. Jesus uses it of the bread-and-word contrast: man lives “by every word that proceeds out of God’s mouth” (Matthew 4:4). In John 15:26 the Spirit is the One “who proceeds from the Father.” He does not originate His own message. He comes from the Father, is sent by the Son, and speaks of the Son. Everything about His coming points away from Himself and toward the Christ He testifies about. The Spirit comes from the Father, is sent by the Son, and speaks of the Son. His whole direction is Christward.

stations.verse: Therefore I make known to you that no man speaking by God’s Spirit says, “Jesus is accursed.” No one can say, “Jesus is Lord,” but by the Holy Spirit.
note: The most basic Christian confession is itself the Spirit’s work. A man cannot truly own Jesus as Lord — not as mere words, but as heart-reality — apart from the Spirit enabling it. This means every genuine bit of your faith in Christ is already evidence of the Spirit within you. He has been pointing you to the Son since before you knew His name.
stations.question: If your ability to call Jesus “Lord” is itself proof of the Spirit’s work in you, how does that change your confidence that He is present and active?
stations.gloss: lord, master; in the LXX chiefly the rendering of the divine name
stations.live: Say “Jesus is Lord” out loud once each morning this week, and thank the Spirit for bringing you to say it.
body: Kyrios means one with power and authority — lord, master. The Greek Old Testament uses it chiefly to render the divine name. So when the first Christians said “Jesus is Lord,” they were saying more than “Jesus is my boss.” They were giving Him the name that belongs to God. Paul says no one can say that and mean it “but by the Holy Spirit.” The confession on your lips is the Spirit’s fingerprint on your soul. The simplest thing you believe about Jesus — that He is Lord — is already the Spirit’s work in you.

stations.verse: But we all, with unveiled face seeing the glory of the Lord as in a mirror, are transformed into the same image from glory to glory, even as from the Lord, the Spirit.
note: This is how the Spirit changes a man: He unveils his face to see the glory of the Lord, and in the seeing the man is changed into the same image. The Spirit’s transforming work is not to make you stare harder at your sin, but to lift your eyes to the glory of Christ — and in the seeing, you are remade, “from glory to glory.”
stations.question: Have you been trying to change by staring at your own failure instead of looking at Christ?
stations.gloss: to show as in a mirror; middle, to see as in a mirror, or to reflect as a mirror
stations.live: Spend ten minutes this week reading one Gospel scene slowly, with no goal but to look at Jesus in it.
body: Katoptrizō appears only here in the New Testament. It comes from katoptron, a mirror. The lexicon allows two readings — seeing as in a mirror, or reflecting like one — and WEB takes the first: “seeing the glory of the Lord as in a mirror.” Either way the picture is a face turned toward the glory of Christ, and the change is done to the man, not by him: he is “transformed … from the Lord, the Spirit.” You become like what you keep looking at. You do not transform yourself by effort. You are transformed by the Spirit as you look at Christ.

stations.verse: But the Counselor, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, will teach you all things, and will remind you of all that I said to you.
note: The Spirit teaches, and His subject is what Jesus said. He “will remind you of all that I said to you.” The Spirit does not bring a new gospel. He brings the old words back — the words of Christ — at the moment a man needs them. Peter learned this the hard way: when the rooster crowed, he remembered the word of the Lord. The Spirit’s reminders always lead back to Jesus.
stations.question: Which word of Jesus has the Spirit been bringing back to your mind lately?
stations.gloss: to cause one to remember, to put one in mind, to remind
stations.live: Memorize one saying of Jesus this week. Ask the Spirit to bring it back when you need it, and write down when He does.
body: Hypomimnēskō means to put someone in mind of something. Peter uses it of his own letter: “I will not be negligent to remind you of these things” (2 Peter 1:12). Luke uses it of Peter in the courtyard: the rooster crowed, and Peter “remembered the Lord’s word” (Luke 22:61). Jesus promises the Spirit “will remind you of all that I said to you.” The Spirit’s memory work is Christ-shaped. He brings back the words of Jesus, often at the moment they cut and heal. The Spirit does not give you a new Jesus. He brings the real one back to mind.

practices.title: REDIRECT THE HUNGER
practices.body: Every time you find yourself wanting a spiritual experience this week, redirect the hunger with a single prayer: “Spirit, I do not want a feeling. I want to see Jesus. Show me the Son.” Test whether Christ grows more real to you when you seek Him this way rather than chasing sensation. The Spirit loves this prayer and delights to answer it.

practices.title: BEHOLD, DON’T STARE AT THE MIRROR
practices.body: Pick the one sin or weakness you most obsess over. This week, stop staring at it. Every time it rises to accuse you, deliberately lift your eyes instead: open the Gospels, read a scene of Jesus, and behold Him. Trust 2 Corinthians 3 — that you are changed not by staring at the failure but by beholding the Lord. Let the Spirit do the transforming.

practices.title: NAME WHAT YOU SEE
practices.body: At the end of each day this week, name one thing the Spirit showed you about Christ — one way Jesus became more real, more merciful, more glorious. Write it down. Watching the list grow across the week is watching the Spirit do His defining work: glorifying the Son before your eyes.

practices.title: LET HIM REMIND YOU
practices.body: The Spirit brings back the words of Jesus. This week, carry one saying of Christ on a card in your pocket — John 16:14 is a good one. Read it at lunch and before sleep. When it comes to mind unasked, stop and thank the Spirit for the reminder.

practices.title: CONFESS HIM OUT LOUD
practices.body: No one says “Jesus is Lord” but by the Holy Spirit. Find one natural moment this week — at the table, with a friend, with your children — to say plainly what Jesus means to you. One sentence is enough. Let the Spirit who gave you the confession give you the words.

title: The Spirit Who Points to Christ
subtitle: His central work: He will glorify Me
keyVerse: He will glorify me, for he will take from what is mine, and will declare it to you.

passage.text: “When the Counselor has come, whom I will send to you from the Father, the Spirit of truth, who proceeds from the Father, he will testify about me.
“I still have many things to tell you, but you can’t bear them now.

However when he, the Spirit of truth, has come, he will guide you into all truth, for he will not speak from himself; but whatever he hears, he will speak. He will declare to you things that are coming.
He will glorify me, for he will take from what is mine, and will declare it to you.
All things that the Father has are mine; therefore I said that he takes of mine and will declare it to you.
Therefore I make known to you that no man speaking by God’s Spirit says, “Jesus is accursed.” No one can say, “Jesus is Lord,” but by the Holy Spirit.
Now the Lord is the Spirit and where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is liberty.
But we all, with unveiled face seeing the glory of the Lord as in a mirror, are transformed into the same image from glory to glory, even as from the Lord, the Spirit.

stationsIntro: The verses below show, from every angle, that the Spirit’s central work is to glorify, witness to, confess, and reveal Christ — and to change a man by making him behold Him. Read each slowly. Let the commentary land before you answer. Then sit with the word study beneath it. The thread this week runs from chasing the Spirit to seeing the Son — and being changed in the seeing.
lifeIntro: This week is about reorienting your whole pursuit of the Spirit toward Christ. The point of Week 2 is to stop chasing the Spirit as an end and start asking Him to reveal the Son. Five practices for the next seven days.
prayer: Spirit of truth, I have chased feelings and called it seeking You. Turn my eyes from the experience to the Son. Take what belongs to Jesus and declare it to me. Remind me of His words when I forget them. Let me see His glory, and change me as I look. Father, thank You for sending the Spirit who points to Christ. Lord Jesus, be larger to me this week than last. I confess You as Lord, and I thank You that I can. Amen.
prayerLines: Spirit of truth, I have chased feelings and called it seeking You.
Turn my eyes from the experience to the Son.
Take what belongs to Jesus and declare it to me.
Remind me of His words when I forget them.
Let me see His glory, and change me as I look.
Father, thank You for sending the Spirit who points to Christ.
Lord Jesus, be larger to me this week than last.
I confess You as Lord, and I thank You that I can. Amen.
bottomLine: The Spirit’s whole work is to glorify Christ. He does not want to be chased as a feeling. He wants to show you the Son, and as you look at the Son, He changes you into His likeness.
benediction: Brother, there is a way to seek the Holy Spirit that the Spirit Himself will not bless — and many sincere men are stuck in it. They chase the Spirit as an experience, a feeling, a power for its own sake, going from high to high, and wondering why the highs fade and the dust returns. They are chasing the wind. And the reason they cannot catch it is that they are seeking the Spirit as the destination, when the Spirit is the guide — and the destination He is guiding them to is Christ.

Because the Spirit has one great passion, and it is not Himself. “He will glorify me,” Jesus said. The Spirit is a floodlight aimed at the Son, a witness testifying to the Son, the One who takes what belongs to Jesus and makes it real to you. He is the most self-effacing Person in the universe, and His joy is to lift your eyes off Himself and onto Christ — and then, as you behold the glory of the Lord, to change you into that same image, degree by degree, without your even feeling the chisel.

So this week, lift up your eyes — but lift them where the Spirit is pointing. Not at the light, but at what the light reveals. Not at the experience, but at the Son the experience was meant to show you. Not at your own sin in the mirror, but at Christ, whom the Spirit holds before your unveiled face. The Spirit is not asking you to stare at Him. He is turning your face, gently and continually, toward Jesus — because He knows that a man becomes what he beholds, and He means for you to become like the Son.

You do not have to catch the wind. You have to let it carry you where it was always blowing: to Christ. Ask the Spirit for the one thing He loves most to give — a clearer sight of Jesus — and watch the dust lose its grip as the Son fills your view. The Spirit points to Christ. Follow where He points, and you will find yourself revived.
closingVerse: The Spirit will not be chased as a destination. He will only be followed as a guide — and He is always guiding you to Jesus. Stop chasing the wind. Follow it to Christ.
carry: What would change this week if you asked the Spirit only to show you Jesus?

sections.heading: SOUL DUST TO REVIVAL
pulls: The Word is the riverbed. The Spirit is the river. A man can study the bed for years and stay dry. He is revived when the water comes.
paras: A man can know the Bible well and still be dry. Underneath that dryness is a question: what makes the Word come alive in a man? A man can read the living Word and still feel nothing. He can store it, study it, even love it, and still wake up dry. The Word is the riverbed. This week meets the river itself.

Jesus stands up on the last day of the feast and shouts an invitation that sounds a lot like the dust: if anyone thirsts. He is not speaking to people who have it together. He is speaking to the parched — and He promises that the one who comes to Him and drinks will not merely be wetted but will become a source: “from within him will flow rivers of living water.” And John says plainly what He meant: “he said this about the Spirit.”

That is the turn this whole week makes. The dust is dryness — a soul cracked and parched, clinging to dirt because there is no water in it. And the answer is not more effort to stay moist. It is the Spirit, poured into a man until he is not just watered but flowing. Revive me according to Your word and come to Me and drink are the same cry from two angles: the dry man asking to be filled, and the Lord offering the only thing that fills him — the living water of His own Spirit.

sections.heading: WHAT THIS WEEK IS AFTER
paras: This week goes after the Spirit Himself, not just the effects men want from Him. A lot of men want the fruit — peace, power, self-control — without wanting the Person who produces it. They treat the Spirit like a force to be tapped instead of a Counselor to be welcomed. John 7 and John 14 will not allow it. The living water is the Spirit; the Counselor is a Person the Father gives to be with a man and in him forever.

The goal this week is to come thirsty to Christ and receive the Spirit He pours out — to stop trying to manufacture your own moisture and let the river flow. Every road runs to Christ, and this one runs straight through Him, because it is from Christ that the Spirit is given. The thirsty man does not go around Jesus to find the water. He comes to Jesus and drinks, and the Spirit He gives becomes a spring inside.

sections.heading: WHY THESE CHAPTERS
paras: Because John 7 and John 14 hold the two halves of the Spirit’s coming. John 7 gives the promise — thirst, come, drink, and rivers will flow — but adds that the Spirit had not yet been given, because Jesus was not yet glorified. John 14 is where the promise turns to a named gift: the Counselor, the Spirit of truth, who will be with the disciples forever, teaching them, reminding them, and making His home in them. Promise, then Person. The dry man is not given a technique. He is given Someone.

sections.heading: The Man Trying to Stay Moist
paras: You know the exhausting work of it. A man feels the dryness and tries to manage it himself — a little more discipline, a better routine, a conference high, a worship playlist to keep the feeling going. He is forever trying to stay moist by his own effort, topping himself off, and forever drying out again because there is no spring inside, only what he can pour in from outside. Jesus offers the opposite of self-watering. He offers an internal spring — the Spirit — so the man is not desperately maintaining moisture but flowing from a source that does not run dry. Stop trying to stay wet. Come and drink.

parts.label: PART ONE
parts.heading: Come and Drink
paras: Notice how Jesus frames the invitation. Not if anyone is worthy. Not if anyone has cleaned himself up. Just if anyone thirsts. The only qualification is the dryness itself. This is the same logic as Isaiah’s free invitation — “Come, everyone who thirsts” — and it lands on the same kind of man: the one parched enough to admit it.

And the promise is staggering. The thirsty man who comes and drinks does not just get his own thirst quenched. He becomes a riverhead: “from within him will flow rivers of living water.” Not a trickle. Not a private sip. Rivers, plural, flowing outward. The Spirit does not merely top a man off; He turns the dry man into a source of water for others. The most parched man in the room, once he drinks, becomes the one the water flows through.

parts.label: PART TWO
parts.heading: The Counselor Who Stays
paras: In John 14, the promise gets a name and a permanence. Jesus tells the disciples He will ask the Father, “and he will give you another Counselor, that he may be with you forever.” The Counselor is a Person called to a man’s side — comfort that turns out to be Someone, not a feeling. The Spirit is that Person, and the key word is forever.

This matters enormously for the dust. A man’s experience of God often feels like weather — close one week, distant the next, watered on Sunday and parched by Wednesday. Jesus promises something steadier than weather: a Counselor who comes to be with you and, He says, “will be in you.” Not a visitor who comes and goes with your moods, but a resident who has moved in to stay. The dryness you feel is not the Spirit leaving. He does not leave. He stays.

And notice what this Counselor does. He teaches you all things and brings to your remembrance all that Christ has said. That is the link between the Spirit and the Word. The Spirit is the One who takes the Word you have stored — hidden in your heart — and brings it back up at the moment you need it, makes it land, makes it live. The Word is the riverbed; the Spirit is the river; and the Spirit is also the one who reminds you where the riverbed is. He does not work apart from the Word. He makes the Word flow.

stations.verse: Now on the last and greatest day of the feast, Jesus stood and cried out, “If anyone is thirsty, let him come to me and drink!
note: The only qualification is thirst. Jesus does not call the impressive or the put-together; He calls the parched. He stands on the last and greatest day of the feast and cries it out loud: “If anyone is thirsty, let him come to me and drink!” The dust is dryness; the answer is to come to Christ and drink.
stations.question: Where are you most parched right now?
stations.gloss: to thirst; figuratively, to thirst for
stations.live: Write one sentence naming your thirst plainly. Pray it each morning this week: “Lord, I am thirsty. I come to You to drink.”
body: Dipsaō is plain thirst — the body’s need for water. Jesus uses it of the blessed who “hunger and thirst after righteousness” (Matthew 5:6). John uses it of Jesus on the cross: “I am thirsty” (John 19:28). The One who cried “If anyone is thirsty” knew thirst Himself. He does not require fullness as the price of admission. He requires thirst — the very emptiness the dust produces. The one qualification for the living water is the dryness you were ashamed of.

stations.verse: He who believes in me, as the Scripture has said, from within him will flow rivers of living water.” But he said this about the Spirit, which those believing in him were to receive. For the Holy Spirit was not yet given, because Jesus wasn’t yet glorified.
note: The promise overshoots the need — the thirsty man does not just get a drink, he becomes a river. And John steps in so there is no mistaking it: the living water is the Spirit. The river Jesus promises is not an experience, a feeling, or a technique. It is a Person, received. Everything that revives the dry man traces to the Spirit poured into him.
stations.question: Have you thought of being revived as getting a feeling back, or as receiving the Spirit Himself?
stations.gloss: a river, a stream, a torrent
stations.live: When you feel dry this week, read John 7:37–39 aloud and ask the Spirit to flow where you feel empty.
body: Potamos is a river — a running stream, sometimes a torrent that beats against a house (Matthew 7:25). Jesus uses the plural: “rivers of living water.” Not a cup. Not a trickle. John explains it at once: “he said this about the Spirit.” And the last chapter of the Bible opens on the same picture: “a river of water of life” flowing from the throne (Revelation 22:1). The Spirit in a believer is a foretaste of that river. God does not give the thirsty man a cup to ration. He gives him a river.

stations.verse: I will pray to the Father, and he will give you another Counselor, that he may be with you forever: the Spirit of truth, whom the world can’t receive; for it doesn’t see him and doesn’t know him. You know him, for he lives with you, and will be in you.
note: Here the living water gets a name and a permanence: the Counselor, given “that he may be with you forever,” who “will be in you.” A man’s sense of God may rise and fall like weather, but the Spirit is not weather. He is a resident, not a visitor. The dryness a man feels is not the Spirit departing. He stays, even when the feeling does not.
stations.question: Do you live as if the Spirit comes and goes with your moods?
stations.gloss: an age, a period of time; in the phrase eis ton aiōna, forever
stations.live: Each time you feel far from God this week, say: “The Counselor is with me forever. He has not moved.”
body: Aiōn is a span of time — an age — and in the phrase Jesus uses here, it means forever. The Counselor is given “that he may be with you forever.” The same phrase closes the bread of life promise: whoever eats this bread “will live forever” (John 6:51). The Spirit’s presence is not a season. It is not tied to how you feel on a Tuesday. It is permanent, because the One who promised it keeps His word. Your feelings are weather. The Spirit is a resident.

stations.verse: and hope doesn’t disappoint us, because God’s love has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who was given to us.
note: Paul shows the river arriving. The Spirit is not given at arm’s length; “God’s love has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit.” The same dry heart that clung to the dust becomes the vessel God fills with His own love. The rivers Jesus promised are, at bottom, the love of God moving into a man who had run dry.
stations.question: Where do you most need God’s love poured into you rather than worked up by you?
stations.gloss: to pour out; metaphorically, of the Spirit poured out
stations.live: Read Romans 5:5 each morning this week and thank God for one specific way He has poured His love on you.
body: Ekcheō is the verb for pouring out — wine from a skin, blood from a wound. Jesus uses it of His own blood “poured out for many” (Matthew 26:28). Peter uses it of Pentecost: “I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh” (Acts 2:17). Paul uses it here of God’s love “poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit.” God does not measure His love out by the drop. He pours it — and the cup Christ poured out is the reason the Spirit can be poured in. The Spirit does not ration the love of God. He floods a dry heart with it.

stations.verse: For I will pour water on him who is thirsty, and streams on the dry ground. I will pour my Spirit on your descendants, and my blessing on your offspring:
note: Centuries before the feast in John 7, God made the same promise through Isaiah: water on the thirsty, streams on dry ground, and in the same breath, “I will pour my Spirit.” The picture is not a drip. It is a downpour on cracked earth. The promise is spoken to a people who had failed, and it rests on God’s word, not their record.
stations.question: What part of your life looks most like dry ground right now?
stations.gloss: to pour, to pour out, to flow, to cast
stations.live: Find one dry place outside this week — a cracked path, a dusty yard. Stand there a moment and pray Isaiah 44:3 over your own heart.
body: Yāṣaq is to pour — oil on a king’s head (1 Samuel 10:1), water over a prophet’s hands (2 Kings 3:11). In Isaiah 44:3 God uses it of Himself: “I will pour water on him who is thirsty … I will pour my Spirit on your descendants.” The one doing the pouring is God. The ground does nothing but lie there dry. The man in the dust does not have to produce the rain. He only has to be dry ground under a pouring God. Dry ground does not water itself. It waits under a God who pours.

practices.title: NAME THE THIRST
practices.body: Jesus’ only qualification was thirst. This week, name yours plainly to God. Where are you dry — prayerless, joyless, going through motions? Do not try to fix it first. Pray simply: “Lord, I am thirsty. I come to You to drink.” The naming of the thirst is the coming. Do it daily.

practices.title: STOP SELF-WATERING
practices.body: Identify one way you try to manufacture your own spiritual moisture — a high you chase, a feeling you engineer, an effort you exhaust yourself with. This week, lay it down once and instead ask the Spirit to be the spring: “I cannot keep myself wet. Be the river in me.” Notice the difference between striving for moisture and receiving it.

practices.title: TRUST THE RESIDENT, NOT THE WEATHER
practices.body: When the dryness comes this week and it feels like God has left, preach John 14 to yourself: the Counselor is in you, forever, not weather that comes and goes. Put a hand on that promise out loud: “The Spirit lives in me even now, even when I feel nothing.” Trust the resident over the feeling.

practices.title: TAKE THE PROMISE TO THE DRY PLACE
practices.body: Isaiah 44:3 promises water on the thirsty and the Spirit poured out. Write the verse on a card and put it where your dryness usually shows up — the truck, the desk, the nightstand. Each time you see it, pray it back to God in your own words.

practices.title: LET ONE STREAM FLOW OUT
practices.body: Jesus said rivers would flow from within the man who drinks. This week, let one small stream flow toward someone else: a word of encouragement, a meal, a call to a man you know is dry. Do it as a man who has been given water, not as one trying to earn it.

title: Rivers of Living Water
subtitle: the Spirit poured into the thirsty
keyVerse: “Now on the last and greatest day of the feast, Jesus stood and cried out, “If anyone is thirsty, let him come to me and drink! He who believes in me, as the Scripture has said, from within him will flow rivers of living water.””

passage.text: Now on the last and greatest day of the feast, Jesus stood and cried out, “If anyone is thirsty, let him come to me and drink!
He who believes in me, as the Scripture has said, from within him will flow rivers of living water.”
But he said this about the Spirit, which those believing in him were to receive. For the Holy Spirit was not yet given, because Jesus wasn’t yet glorified.
If you love me, keep my commandments.
I will pray to the Father, and he will give you another Counselor, that he may be with you forever:
the Spirit of truth, whom the world can’t receive; for it doesn’t see him and doesn’t know him. You know him, for he lives with you, and will be in you.
I will not leave you orphans. I will come to you.
Yet a little while, and the world will see me no more; but you will see me. Because I live, you will live also.
In that day you will know that I am in my Father, and you in me, and I in you.
One who has my commandments and keeps them, that person is one who loves me. One who loves me will be loved by my Father, and I will love him, and will reveal myself to him.”
Judas (not Iscariot) said to him, “Lord, what has happened that you are about to reveal yourself to us, and not to the world?”
Jesus answered him, “If a man loves me, he will keep my word. My Father will love him, and we will come to him, and make our home with him.
He who doesn’t love me doesn’t keep my words. The word which you hear isn’t mine, but the Father’s who sent me.
I have said these things to you while still living with you.
But the Counselor, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, will teach you all things, and will remind you of all that I said to you.
Peace I leave with you. My peace I give to you; not as the world gives, I give to you. Don’t let your heart be troubled, neither let it be fearful.

stationsIntro: The verses below move through Jesus’ promise of living water and the gift of the Counselor, and reach to the Scriptures that speak of the Spirit poured into dry hearts. Read each slowly. Let the commentary land before you answer. Then sit with the word study beneath it. The thread now runs from the dust to the river — the dry soul filled and flowing.
lifeIntro: This week the practices are about coming thirsty and learning to receive rather than manufacture. The point of Week 3 is to stop self-watering and come to Christ to drink. Five practices for the next seven days.
prayer: Lord Jesus, I am thirsty, and I have been trying to water myself. I stop. I come to You to drink. Pour Your Spirit on this dry ground. Holy Spirit, You are with me forever — teach me to trust that over my moods. Pour the Father’s love into my heart where it has run dry. Bring back the Word I have stored and make it live. Let what You give me flow out to someone else. Father, thank You for rivers where I deserved dust. Amen.
prayerLines: Lord Jesus, I am thirsty, and I have been trying to water myself.
I stop. I come to You to drink.
Pour Your Spirit on this dry ground.
Holy Spirit, You are with me forever — teach me to trust that over my moods.
Pour the Father’s love into my heart where it has run dry.
Bring back the Word I have stored and make it live.
Let what You give me flow out to someone else.
Father, thank You for rivers where I deserved dust. Amen.
bottomLine: The Spirit is the living water Jesus promised to the thirsty. The only qualification is thirst. He is poured out, not earned, and He stays with you forever, even when you feel nothing.
benediction: Brother, the dust is dryness. That is what it has been all along — a soul cracked and parched, clinging to dirt because there was no water in it. A man can have the whole riverbed of the Word laid out in him and still be dry, because the riverbed is not the river. This week you came to the river — and found it is a Person.

Jesus does not stand at the feast and call the worthy. He calls the thirsty. If anyone thirsts, let him come to Me and drink. The only ticket is the dryness you were ashamed of. And He does not promise to top you off so you can go back to self-watering. He promises a spring inside — the Spirit, poured into you, until the driest man in the room becomes the one rivers of living water flow through. The Counselor comes, and He comes to stay: with you, in you, forever, not weather but resident, not a force but a Person called alongside who will not leave.

So when the dryness comes — and it will — lift up your eyes. Lift them off your exhausting effort to stay moist and onto Christ, who says come and drink. Lift them off the weather of your feelings and onto the Counselor who lives in you when you feel nothing at all. Lift them off your empty container and onto the God who does not ration His love but pours it out by the Spirit until your dry heart is drenched. And lift them, most of all, onto Jesus Himself, from whom the living water flows — because the thirsty man does not find the river by going around Him, but by coming to Him and drinking.

You do not have to work up your own water. You have to come thirsty to Christ and receive the Spirit He pours out — the river that turns a clinging, cracked, dust-bound soul into a flowing one. The Word is the riverbed. The Spirit is the river. Come and drink.
closingVerse: Stop trying to stay wet by your own effort. Come to Christ thirsty, and let the Spirit be the spring. The dry man who drinks becomes a river.
carry: Where would you let the Spirit flow if you stopped trying to stay wet on your own?

sections.heading: SOUL DUST TO REVIVAL
pulls: You did not make yourself a Christian any more than you made yourself born. The Spirit raised you from the dead. Revival is just Him doing again what He did first.
paras: The Spirit is a Person, and His great work is to reveal Christ. Now go back to the very beginning — because the first thing the Spirit ever does in a man is the most dramatic thing that can happen to a human being: He raises the dead. Not improves. Not motivates. Raises. Jesus tells a religious man, at the top of his game, that he must be “born anew” — born of the Spirit — or he will never even see the kingdom.

This is where the dust gets named at its root. The dust is not just dryness or weariness. In its deepest layer, the natural man is dead — dead in trespasses, unable to revive himself, as unable to make himself alive as a corpse is to climb out of a grave. And into that deadness the Spirit comes and does what only God can do: He gives new life. He takes a stony heart and gives a heart of flesh. He breathes on dry bones until they stand up and live. The word for it is regeneration — being born all over again, from above, by the Spirit.

This reframes revive me according to Your word entirely. Revival, at its deepest, is not a technique or a mood. It is resurrection. The same Spirit who first made you alive is the One who keeps breathing life into the dry places. A man does not revive himself any more than he birthed himself. He was born of the Spirit — and the Spirit who began that life is the only One who can renew it.

sections.heading: WHAT THIS WEEK IS AFTER
paras: This week goes after the truth that new life is God’s work, not yours — because it changes everything about how a man walks with God. If a man believes he made himself alive, he will spend his life trying to keep himself alive by effort, and he will exhaust himself. But if he sees that the Spirit birthed him, he learns to depend on the Spirit for the life he could never generate. The whole posture of the Christian life shifts from self-manufacture to reliance.

The goal this week is to see clearly that you were raised from death to life by the Spirit — and to rest the whole weight of your revival on the One who did it. This too points to Christ: it is by union with the risen Jesus that the Spirit makes a man alive. The new birth is not a self-help upgrade. It is being joined to the living Christ by the living Spirit, so that His resurrection life becomes yours. You are not renovating a corpse. You have been raised.

sections.heading: WHY THESE PASSAGES
paras: Because they show the new birth from every side. In John 3, Jesus makes it non-negotiable — you must be born of the Spirit or you cannot even see the kingdom. In Ezekiel 36, God promises the mechanism — a new heart, a new spirit, His Spirit put within His people, stone traded for flesh. In Ezekiel 37, He dramatizes it — a valley of dry bones brought to life when the Spirit breathes. And in Titus 3, Paul names it — saved by the washing of regeneration and renewal of the Holy Spirit. Command, promise, picture, and doctrine, all saying one thing: the Spirit raises the dead.

sections.heading: The Man Renovating a Corpse
paras: You know the exhaustion, if you have ever tried it. A man treats the Christian life as a renovation project — patching up the old self, improving his habits, managing his sin, sanding down his rough edges. And he cannot understand why it never holds, why the same failures keep returning, why he is so tired. It is because you cannot renovate a corpse into a living man. No amount of improvement turns death into life. What the natural man needs is not renovation but resurrection — and that is precisely what the Spirit gives. The moment a man stops trying to fix the old self and starts depending on the new life the Spirit birthed in him, the futile renovation ends and real life begins.

parts.label: PART ONE
parts.heading: You Must Be Born Again
paras: Nicodemus was the best religious man of his day — a Pharisee, a ruler, a teacher of Israel. And Jesus tells him, of all people, that none of it is enough: “unless one is born anew, he can’t see God’s Kingdom.” Not reform again. Not try harder again. Born again — an event as far outside a man’s control as his first birth was. You did not arrange your own conception; you cannot arrange your own regeneration. It is done to you, by the Spirit, from above.

This is devastating to the self-made man and freeing to the exhausted one. Everything Nicodemus had built — his discipline, his knowledge, his religious résumé — Jesus set aside with a single requirement Nicodemus could not meet on his own. The kingdom is not entered by the polished flesh. It is entered by those the Spirit has made new. And that is good news for a man in the dust, because it means his hope was never his own performance. It was always the Spirit’s power to give life.

parts.label: PART TWO
parts.heading: A New Heart, and Breath in Dry Bones
paras: Long before Jesus met Nicodemus, God had promised exactly this through Ezekiel, and the promise is exact: “I will also give you a new heart, and I will put a new spirit within you. I will take away the stony heart out of your flesh, and I will give you a heart of flesh.” And I will put my Spirit within you, and cause you to walk in my statutes. Read what God takes responsibility for. The new heart — His doing. The new spirit — His gift. The removal of the stone — His surgery. His Spirit within — His initiative. Even the walking in obedience — He causes it. From first to last, it is God’s work by God’s Spirit.

Then, in the next chapter, God turns the promise into an unforgettable picture. Ezekiel stands in a valley full of dry bones — the deadest image imaginable, bleached bones scattered on the ground — and God asks, can these bones live? Then He commands the prophet to prophesy, and the Spirit breathes, and the bones come together, and flesh forms, and breath enters them, and a vast army stands to its feet, alive. That valley is the natural man. That breath is the Spirit. And that resurrection is what happened to you.

This is the answer to the dust at its deepest. When a man feels most like a valley of dry bones — scattered, lifeless, beyond repair — the honest question is God’s own: can these bones live? And the answer is the Spirit’s specialty. He does not ask the bones to revive themselves. He breathes, and the dead live. The same Spirit who first raised you when you were dead in your sins is present now to breathe again on whatever in you has gone dry. Revival is resurrection, and resurrection is what the Spirit does.

stations.verse: That which is born of the flesh is flesh. That which is born of the Spirit is spirit. Don’t marvel that I said to you, ‘You must be born anew.’
note: The flesh can only reproduce flesh; only the Spirit produces spiritual life. This is why self-improvement never crosses the gap — a dead man cannot upgrade himself into a living one. New life is a birth, not an achievement, and it comes from above, by the Spirit. The requirement is absolute, and so is the good news: what you cannot do, the Spirit does.
stations.question: Where are you most exhausted from renovating what only resurrection can fix?
stations.gloss: from above; from the beginning; hence anew, again
stations.live: Each morning this week, before you ask God for anything, thank Him that your life with Him started from above, not from you.
body: Anōthen can mean “from above” and “anew.” John uses it plainly for “from above” elsewhere: the One “who comes from above is above all” (John 3:31). WEB renders it “born anew” in John 3:7, and the lexicon notes that most take it that way here. Either way the direction is the point. New life does not rise from the man. It comes down to him, a second birth that begins with God. A man does not climb up into new life. It comes down to him.

stations.verse: I will also give you a new heart, and I will put a new spirit within you. I will take away the stony heart out of your flesh, and I will give you a heart of flesh.
note: Every verb belongs to God. He gives the new heart, puts the new spirit within, takes away the stony heart, gives a heart of flesh. The man contributes nothing but the stone. This is the surgery of regeneration — God trading a heart that could not feel or respond for one that can. A hard, stony heart is not filed down by effort. It is removed and replaced, by God.
stations.question: Where does your heart still feel like stone toward God?
stations.gloss: flesh; the body; kindred; mankind; flesh as frail
stations.live: Name one place you have gone numb toward God. Pray Ezekiel 36:26 over that exact place every day this week.
body: Bāśār is flesh — the body, the stuff a man is made of. It can mean human frailty: “All flesh is like grass” (Isaiah 40:6). In Ezekiel 36:26 it is the soft, living tissue God puts where stone used to be: “I will give you a heart of flesh.” Not flesh as sinful nature here, but a heart that can feel, respond, and love. God trades the heart that could not feel Him for one that can. A stone heart cannot be taught to feel. It has to be replaced, and God is the surgeon.

stations.verse: The Lord Yahweh says to these bones: “Behold, I will cause breath to enter into you, and you will live. I will lay sinews on you, and will bring up flesh on you, and cover you with skin, and put breath in you, and you will live. Then you will know that I am Yahweh.” ’
note: The valley of dry bones is the natural man, and the breath is the Spirit. God does not ask the bones to assemble themselves. He speaks, and sinew, flesh, skin, and breath come in order, until the dead stand up alive. However dead a man feels — scattered, dry, beyond repair — the question God asked Ezekiel is His own to answer: “can these bones live?” By the Spirit, yes.
stations.question: What part of your life feels like a valley of dry bones right now?
stations.gloss: bone, limb; substance, self
stations.live: Write down one thing in your life that looks dead. Read Ezekiel 37:1–10 over it, and leave the outcome with God.
body: ʿEṣem is bone — the hard frame of a body, and by extension the self. Adam used it of Eve: “bone of my bones” (Genesis 2:23). In Ezekiel 37 the bones are dry, scattered, “very dry,” and God speaks to them directly: “I will cause breath to enter into you, and you will live.” The bones do nothing. God lays sinew, brings flesh, covers skin, and puts breath in. Resurrection is God’s work from the frame outward. God does not ask dry bones to try harder. He speaks to them, and they live.

stations.verse: not by works of righteousness which we did ourselves, but according to his mercy, he saved us through the washing of regeneration and renewing by the Holy Spirit,
note: Paul names the doctrine plainly: God “saved us through the washing of regeneration and renewing by the Holy Spirit,” and He did it “according to his mercy,” not by works of righteousness. The new birth is a washing and a renewing, done to a man by the Spirit. Nothing here is earned. It is mercy, applied by the Spirit, making dead men new.
stations.question: Do you rest your standing with God on His mercy or on your own performance?
stations.gloss: new birth, renewal, restoration, regeneration
stations.live: Read Titus 3:4–7 this week and underline every word that belongs to God rather than to you.
body: Palingenesia joins palin, again, and genesis, birth or origin. It appears only twice in the New Testament. In Matthew 19:28 it names the renewal of all things when the Son of Man sits on His throne. In Titus 3:5 it names what the Spirit has already done in a single believer: “the washing of regeneration.” The new birth in you is a preview of the new creation to come. The Spirit does not patch the old life. He begins a new one. What God will do for the whole world, He has already begun in you.

stations.verse: Of his own will he gave birth to us by the word of truth, that we should be a kind of first fruits of his creatures.
note: James uses birth language for salvation, and he puts the will in the right place: “Of his own will he gave birth to us.” Not by your will. His. And He did it “by the word of truth” — the Spirit’s instrument is the Word. A man does not arrange his own birth. He wakes up alive because God wanted him alive.
stations.question: How does it change your week to know God wanted you alive before you ever wanted Him?
stations.gloss: to bring forth, to give birth to
stations.live: When temptation starts to “conceive” this week, stop and say James 1:18 aloud. Remember whose family you were born into.
body: Apokyeō is a birth word, used of delivery at the end of pregnancy. James uses it twice, and the contrast is sharp. In 1:15 lust conceives and “bears sin,” and sin “produces death.” In 1:18 God, “of his own will,” gives birth to His people “by the word of truth.” Two births, two families. The dust breeds death. God brings forth life, and He does it because He wills to. Sin gives birth to death. God, by His own will, gives birth to you.

practices.title: STOP RENOVATING
practices.body: Identify the one area where you have been trying hardest to fix the old self by effort — the habit you keep white-knuckling, the sin you keep managing. This week, stop renovating. Instead, pray: “Spirit, I cannot make this alive. You raised me once; breathe life here again.” Depend on resurrection where you have been attempting renovation.

practices.title: NAME THE DRY BONES
practices.body: Name the valley of dry bones in your life right now — the dead place, the hopeless situation, the part of you that feels beyond repair. Bring it deliberately to the Spirit and ask God’s own question over it: can these bones live? Then wait on the One whose specialty is breathing life into exactly what looks finished.

practices.title: REST IN THE GIFT
practices.body: This week, every time you catch yourself trying to earn your standing with God, stop and preach Titus 3 to yourself: “I was saved by mercy, through the washing of regeneration, by the Spirit — not by my performance.” Let the truth that your new life was pure gift settle you. You cannot lose by failure what you never gained by effort.

practices.title: LET THE WORD DO ITS WORK
practices.body: James says God gave you birth “by the word of truth.” The Spirit uses the Word to give life, and He still does. This week, read John 3:1–8 three times, slowly, on three different days. Ask the Spirit each time to breathe on it, and write down one sentence that lands.

practices.title: PRAY FOR ONE DEAD MAN
practices.body: Only the Spirit gives new birth, which means no man is beyond it. Name one person you have written off as hopeless. Pray for him by name every day this week: “Spirit, breathe on him as You breathed on me.”

title: Born of the Spirit
subtitle: raised from death to life
keyVerse: “Jesus answered, “Most certainly I tell you, unless one is born of water and spirit, he can’t enter into God’s Kingdom.”

passage.text: Now there was a man of the Pharisees named Nicodemus, a ruler of the Jews.
The same came to him by night, and said to him, “Rabbi, we know that you are a teacher come from God, for no one can do these signs that you do, unless God is with him.”
Jesus answered him, “Most certainly, I tell you, unless one is born anew, he can’t see God’s Kingdom.”
Nicodemus said to him, “How can a man be born when he is old? Can he enter a second time into his mother’s womb, and be born?”
Jesus answered, “Most certainly I tell you, unless one is born of water and spirit, he can’t enter into God’s Kingdom.
That which is born of the flesh is flesh. That which is born of the Spirit is spirit.
Don’t marvel that I said to you, ‘You must be born anew.’
The wind blows where it wants to, and you hear its sound, but don’t know where it comes from and where it is going. So is everyone who is born of the Spirit.”
I will also give you a new heart, and I will put a new spirit within you. I will take away the stony heart out of your flesh, and I will give you a heart of flesh.
I will put my Spirit within you, and cause you to walk in my statutes. You will keep my ordinances and do them.
Yahweh’s hand was on me, and he brought me out in Yahweh’s Spirit, and set me down in the middle of the valley; and it was full of bones.
