This is the widest reach of revival, and it is the note the whole series has been building toward. The man revived from the dust is not sent only to people like himself. He is sent across borders — to the family member he had written off, the coworker he avoids, the kind of person he assumed was beyond reach, the neighbor whose dust looks different from his own. The Spirit who crossed every line in Acts crosses them still, and He sends filled men across them carrying the same living water they were given.

And there is a tender thing for a man finishing this study. He was, not long ago, the one face-down in the dust, the one who needed someone to come close and not flinch. Now the Spirit fills him to be that someone for another. The cure he received becomes the cure he carries. The dust he was lifted from becomes the dust he kneels beside in someone else, no longer as a fellow casualty but as a witness — a man who can say, I was where you are, and the Spirit revived me according to the Word, and He will do it for you.

stations.verse: But you will receive power when the Holy Spirit has come upon you. You will be witnesses to me in Jerusalem, in all Judea and Samaria, and to the uttermost parts of the earth.
note: The hinge of the whole book of Acts. The Spirit comes first — “when the Holy Spirit has come upon you” — and then the power and the witness. The witness moves outward in widening rings, from Jerusalem “to the uttermost parts of the earth.” The Spirit was never given to be hoarded. He was given to send.
stations.question: Have you wanted the Spirit’s filling mainly for your own comfort?
stations.gloss: to come to, to arrive; to come upon
stations.live: Before you talk with anyone about Christ this week, pray Acts 1:8 over yourself and ask the Spirit to come upon you.
body: Eperchomai means to come upon. The lexicon notes it is used of the Holy Spirit twice: in Luke 1:35, when the angel tells Mary, “The Holy Spirit will come on you,” and in Acts 1:8, “when the Holy Spirit has come upon you.” The same Spirit who came upon Mary to bring Christ into the world comes upon the church to carry Christ out into it. The coming is His. The going follows. The Spirit comes upon you before He sends you out. The power is His first.

stations.verse: Now when the day of Pentecost had come, they were all with one accord in one place. Suddenly there came from the sky a sound like the rushing of a mighty wind, and it filled all the house where they were sitting. Tongues like fire appeared and were distributed to them, and one sat on each of them. They were all filled with the Holy Spirit, and began to speak with other languages, as the Spirit gave them the ability to speak.
note: Pentecost. The Spirit comes with a sound like wind and tongues like fire, and the immediate result is not a private glow but speech — the filled disciples speaking so every nation present hears. The filling moves outward within minutes. This is the pattern for the whole book: the Spirit fills, and the filled go out and tell.
stations.question: When God has moved you, has it stayed private or reached others?
stations.gloss: to fill
stations.live: Ask the Spirit each morning this week to fill you, and ask Him who you should speak to that day.
body: Pimplēmi is to fill. Luke uses it again and again for the Spirit filling people: Elizabeth “was filled with the Holy Spirit” (Luke 1:41), the disciples at Pentecost (Acts 2:4), and the same disciples again after prayer (Acts 4:31). A filled vessel does not stay still when it is moved. It spills. In Luke’s account, the filling is almost always followed by speech — the Spirit fills a man, and the man speaks. The Spirit fills a man to the brim, and a brimful man spills when he is moved.

stations.verse: When they had prayed, the place was shaken where they were gathered together. They were all filled with the Holy Spirit, and they spoke the word of God with boldness.
note: A second filling, and the same result: “they spoke the word of God with boldness.” These are the same men already filled at Pentecost — the filling is not a one-time event but a renewable supply. When the boldness drains, a man does not have to manufacture courage. He prays, and is filled again, and speaks.
stations.question: Where has your boldness drained away and needs to be filled again?
stations.gloss: freedom of speech, plainness, openness, boldness
stations.live: Tell one person this week, in plain words, one thing God has done in you during this study.
body: Parrēsia is built from pas, all, and rhēsis, speech — speaking everything, plainly, without holding back. The rulers saw it in Peter and John and “marveled” that unlearned men spoke with it (Acts 4:13). Paul uses it: “we use great boldness of speech” (2 Corinthians 3:12). The dust taught a man to hide, mask, and manage. The Spirit fills him with freedom to speak plainly of what God has done. The man the dust taught to hide, the Spirit fills with boldness to speak.

stations.verse: The Spirit said to Philip, “Go near, and join yourself to this chariot.
note: The Spirit does not send Philip to a crowd. He sends him to one man in one chariot on a desert road. “Go near, and join yourself to this chariot.” Mission in Acts is often that small: one man, one conversation, one open question about a passage of Scripture. Philip ran, listened, and began with the text the man was already reading.
stations.question: Who is the one man the Spirit may be telling you to go near to this week?
stations.gloss: to glue together; to join firmly; to cleave to
stations.live: Name one man you know who is in the dust. Go near him this week — a meal, a call, a visit — and simply be with him.
body: Kollaō comes from kolla, glue, and means to join firmly. The lexicon notes the Greek Old Testament uses it chiefly for the Hebrew dāḇaq, the verb of Psalm 119:25, “My soul clings to the dust.” Paul uses it for the believer joined to the Lord (1 Corinthians 6:17). In Acts 8:29 the Spirit uses it of Philip: “join yourself to this chariot.” The soul that once clung to the dust is sent to cling close to another man in need. The man who once clung to the dust is sent to draw close to another man still in it.

stations.verse: As they served the Lord and fasted, the Holy Spirit said, “Separate Barnabas and Saul for me, for the work to which I have called them.” Then, when they had fasted and prayed and laid their hands on them, they sent them away.
note: The sending becomes explicit: the Spirit Himself says “Separate Barnabas and Saul for me,” and the church sends them. It is the Spirit who starts the mission — not human ambition, not guilt, not a recruitment drive. The same Spirit who fills is the One who sends, and He sends men toward people who have never heard.
stations.question: Is there a person the Spirit may be setting you apart to reach?
stations.gloss: to mark off by boundaries; to separate; to set apart for a purpose
stations.live: Ask the Spirit this week: “What have You set me apart for?” Write down what comes, and talk it over with a brother.
body: Aphorizō means to mark off, to set apart for a purpose. Paul uses it of himself: “set apart for the Good News of God” (Romans 1:1), and says God “separated me from my mother’s womb” (Galatians 1:15). In Acts 13:2 the Spirit says, “Separate Barnabas and Saul for me.” The sent man is not self-appointed. He is set apart by the Spirit for work the Spirit has already called him to. You are not sent on your own authority. The Spirit sets you apart and sends you.

practices.title: TRACE THE WHOLE TWELVE WEEKS
practices.body: Sit somewhere quiet for forty-five minutes. Look back across all twelve weeks. Under each week’s title, write one sentence: here is what the Spirit did in me. Some will be honest about how little has shifted yet; name the work anyway. Then read the list as one story: a clinging soul, met by the Spirit, shown Christ, revived, and now sent.

practices.title: NAME ONE PERSON
practices.body: Acts always sends the filled man toward someone. This week, name one person still face-down in the dust — a family member, a friend, a coworker — whom the Spirit may be sending you toward. Do not plan a speech. Just ask: “Spirit, send me to them as a witness. Let me tell what You have done in me.” Then look for the open door.

practices.title: ASK TO BE FILLED AND SENT
practices.body: To close the study, pray a deliberate prayer this week, more than once: “Spirit, fill me again — not to keep, but to give. Send me out as a witness, with Your power behind me.” Receive the filling as the early church did, expecting it to move you outward, and walk out the door.

practices.title: GO NEAR ONE MAN
practices.body: The Spirit sent Philip to one chariot. This week, pick one man — not a crowd — and go near. Ask him one question about his life, and listen more than you talk. If a door opens, tell him plainly what the Spirit has done in you.

practices.title: ASK TO BE SET APART
practices.body: The Spirit set apart Barnabas and Saul while the church worshiped and fasted. Set aside one meal this week to pray instead of eat. Ask one question: “Spirit, what have You set me apart for?” Then tell a brother what you heard.

title: Filled and Sent
subtitle: the Spirit fills a man and sends him
keyVerse: But you will receive power when the Holy Spirit has come upon you. You will be witnesses to me in Jerusalem, in all Judea and Samaria, and to the uttermost parts of the earth.

passage.text: Now when the day of Pentecost had come, they were all with one accord in one place.
Suddenly there came from the sky a sound like the rushing of a mighty wind, and it filled all the house where they were sitting.
Tongues like fire appeared and were distributed to them, and one sat on each of them.
They were all filled with the Holy Spirit, and began to speak with other languages, as the Spirit gave them the ability to speak.
But Peter, standing up with the eleven, lifted up his voice, and spoke out to them, “You men of Judea, and all you who dwell at Jerusalem, let this be known to you, and listen to my words.
For these aren’t drunken, as you suppose, seeing it is only the third hour of the day.
But this is what has been spoken through the prophet Joel:
‘It will be in the last days, says God, that I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh. Your sons and your daughters will prophesy. Your young men will see visions. Your old men will dream dreams.
Yes, and on my servants and on my handmaidens in those days, I will pour out my Spirit, and they will prophesy.
I will show wonders in the sky above, and signs on the earth beneath: blood, and fire, and billows of smoke.
The sun will be turned into darkness, and the moon into blood, before the great and glorious day of the Lord comes.
It will be that whoever will call on the name of the Lord will be saved.’
When they had prayed, the place was shaken where they were gathered together. They were all filled with the Holy Spirit, and they spoke the word of God with boldness.
Now when the apostles who were at Jerusalem heard that Samaria had received the word of God, they sent Peter and John to them,
who, when they had come down, prayed for them, that they might receive the Holy Spirit;
for as yet he had fallen on none of them. They had only been baptized in the name of Christ Jesus.
Then they laid their hands on them, and they received the Holy Spirit.
While Peter was still speaking these words, the Holy Spirit fell on all those who heard the word.
They of the circumcision who believed were amazed, as many as came with Peter, because the gift of the Holy Spirit was also poured out on the Gentiles.
For they heard them speaking in other languages and magnifying God. Then Peter answered,
“Can anyone forbid these people from being baptized with water? They have received the Holy Spirit just like us.”
He commanded them to be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ. Then they asked him to stay some days.
Now in the assembly that was at Antioch there were some prophets and teachers: Barnabas, Simeon who was called Niger, Lucius of Cyrene, Manaen the foster brother of Herod the tetrarch, and Saul.
As they served the Lord and fasted, the Holy Spirit said, “Separate Barnabas and Saul for me, for the work to which I have called them.”
Then, when they had fasted and prayed and laid their hands on them, they sent them away.
So, being sent out by the Holy Spirit, they went down to Seleucia. From there they sailed to Cyprus.
While Apollos was at Corinth, Paul, having passed through the upper country, came to Ephesus and found certain disciples.
He said to them, “Did you receive the Holy Spirit when you believed?” They said to him, “No, we haven’t even heard that there is a Holy Spirit.”
He said, “Into what then were you baptized?” They said, “Into John’s baptism.”
Paul said, “John indeed baptized with the baptism of repentance, saying to the people that they should believe in the one who would come after him, that is, in Jesus.”
When they heard this, they were baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus.
When Paul had laid his hands on them, the Holy Spirit came on them and they spoke with other languages and prophesied.
They were about twelve men in all.

stationsIntro: The verses below move through the Spirit’s fillings in Acts — Pentecost, the shaken room, the open door, the sending church — and out to the witness they always produce. Read each slowly. Let the commentary land before you answer. Then sit with the word study beneath it. The thread, as the whole study closes, runs from the dust all the way out the door — a revived man filled and sent.
lifeIntro: This week closes the whole study, so the practices look back across all twelve weeks and then turn outward, toward the sending. The point of Week 12 is to be filled and to go. Five practices for the next seven days.
prayer: Holy Spirit, You met me in the dust, and now You send me. Come upon me again and fill me, not to keep, but to give. Give me boldness to speak plainly of what You have done. Send me near to one man who is still face-down. Set me apart for the work You have called me to. Father, thank You for reviving me according to Your Word. Lord Jesus, let the next man see You in what You did for me. I am filled and sent. Here I go. Amen.
prayerLines: Holy Spirit, You met me in the dust, and now You send me.
Come upon me again and fill me, not to keep, but to give.
Give me boldness to speak plainly of what You have done.
Send me near to one man who is still face-down.
Set me apart for the work You have called me to.
Father, thank You for reviving me according to Your Word.
Lord Jesus, let the next man see You in what You did for me.
I am filled and sent. Here I go. Amen.
bottomLine: The Spirit does not fill a man to keep him on a shelf. He comes upon him, fills him, gives him boldness, and sends him out. The revived man is a witness, sent to tell another man what God has done.
benediction: Brother, this study began with a man face-down, his soul clinging to the dust, with nothing to offer but his thirst. Look where the Spirit has brought him. The Spirit met him as a Person, showed him Christ, gave him living water, raised him, sealed him, and made him a temple. The Spirit kept him in the Vine, walked him out of the flesh, freed him from condemnation, and carried him groaning through the long season. And now, at the last, the Spirit does the thing all of it was for: He fills the man to the brim and sends him out the door.

Because revival was never meant to end in the man. The Spirit does not fill a vessel to keep it on a shelf; He fills it to be poured out. The man revived from the dust becomes the man who carries the cure — across every border, to the family he had given up on, to the neighbor whose dust looks nothing like his own, to the next man face-down where he himself once lay. He goes not as an expert but as a witness, not in his own courage but in the boldness the Spirit gives, not on his own authority but sent by the Spirit with the power of the resurrection behind him. The hidden man has become the man set free to tell.

So as the whole study closes, lift up your eyes. Lift them off your own comfort and onto the people the Spirit is sending you toward. Lift them off the feeling you wanted to keep and onto the river that only stays fresh by flowing. Lift them off your fear of not having the right words and onto the simple witness you will always be able to give — here is what God did in me. Lift them, most of all and one last time, onto Christ — the living Word, the giver of the Spirit, the One who took a soul clinging to the dust and revived it according to His word, and now sends it out to do for another what was done for it.

You will not walk out of this study finished. You will walk out sent. The dust is not the end of your story; it was the beginning. The Word revived you. The Spirit fills you. And now, brother, lift up your eyes — and go.
closingVerse: From a soul clinging to the dust to a witness sent to the ends of the earth — revived according to His Word, filled by the Spirit, and sent. Now go, and carry it to the next man in the dirt.
carry: Who is the one man the Spirit is sending you toward this week?
